scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that media coverage exposes weakness, then argues genuine heroes remain possible; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Today the smallest faults of famous people are broadcast to the entire world within hours.
Some people argue that in this age of intensive media coverage, society can no longer regard any living person as a hero.
I agree that constant coverage exposes human weakness, but I disagree that real heroes have become impossible.
First, it is true that heavy media coverage makes it harder for anyone to seem heroic.
Cameras and reporters now follow famous people everywhere, revealing flaws that once stayed hidden.
For example, beloved athletes and leaders have lost public respect once their private failings appeared in the news.
This shows that endless coverage can quickly tarnish even a shining reputation.
Knowing that a hero is ordinary and flawed can weaken the admiration people once felt.
The media's hunger for scandal can damage almost any famous figure in time.
To this extent, intensive coverage really does make heroism harder to maintain.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why heroes are still possible

sentences.text: Second, however, the claim that no living person can be a hero goes much too far.
A hero is admired not for being perfect but for genuine courage, kindness, or sacrifice.
Consider the firefighters, doctors, and ordinary people who risk everything to help others in danger.
Such acts win deep and lasting respect, no matter how closely the media may look.
Heavy coverage can even spread word of these heroes to millions who would otherwise never know them.
Learning that heroes have flaws can make them more human and inspiring, not less.
Real heroism, then, can survive the brightest spotlight rather than being destroyed by it.
In conclusion, intensive media coverage does expose flaws that once stayed safely hidden.
But this has not made heroes impossible, since true courage and goodness still earn our respect.
We can still honour living heroes, as long as we admire real virtue rather than demand perfection.
